ObjectName.value: Folio of a genealogical register ('Bahi-Khata') of Haridwar for a local village near Kanpur

Categories.value: Family registers|Genealogy in India|PD Old|PD-scan (PD-old-70)|CC-PD-Mark|PD-old missing SDC copyright status|Culture of Haridwar

ImageDescription.value:
Folio of a genealogical register of Haridwar for a local village near Kanpur. This genealogical record records information related to a familial lineage originating from a small, local village near Kanpur. The genealogical registers of Hardiwar are maintained by geographical origin, with various pandits being responsible for certain areas, regions, localities, etc. This system of genealogical registers has been termed: 'Hindu genealogy registers at Haridwar'.

Further information from [1]:

Bahi Khata is a traditional form of a book of records written in scroll form. While it has been traditionally used for keeping accounts, Bahi Khatas or pothis of this nature are kept securely in the holy town of Haridwar (and others) to maintain genealogy records of Hindu families and can date back to several hundred years. These are securely kept with 'Pandas' who are Hindu Brahmin pandits who pass this down generationally through the same family which is associated with a particular genealogy. It is customary to register and update this history with details of all marriages, births and deaths which take place through an extended joint family structure.

ImageDescription.value:
Haridwar from opposite bank of the Ganges, 1866.

Original description:

Photograph of Haridwar from the 'Strachey Collection of Indian Views', taken by Samuel Bourne in 1866. Haridwar, situated in the foothills of the Himalayas is the first major town on the River Ganges at the point where the river flows onto the plains. Blessed by the trinity of Lord Shiva, Vishnu and Brahma, Haridwar has always been a major pilgrimage site for Hindus. The Ganges here is quite calm and clear and the many bathing ghats are always full of people performing their ablutions. The main bathing ghat at Haridwar is Hari-ki-Pari which reputedly contains a footprint of Lord Vishnu embedded in a stone.

Painting of a Brahmin having feast of the shraddha, illustration to the Swapan-Darpan manuscript (book of dreams), Guler school, ca.1800. Collection: Bhuri Singh Museum, Chamba, Himachal Pradesh
Shradh or pitr paksh is a fortnight period in September when Hindus remember their pitr or ancestors by offering prayers and food to Brahmins. It is believed that certain rituals are performed during shradh to appease the souls of the pitr or ancestors, which bring happiness and prosperity at home. To observe the Shradh rituals, food is offered to Brahmins in the name of the deceased ancestors. auspicious rituals are performed by the eldest son of the family. By observing these rituals, thirst and hunger of ancestors' soul are quenched.

ImageDescription.value:
The ghats at Haridwar

Watercolour of the ghats at Haridwar from 'Views by Seeta Ram from Mohumdy to Gheen Vol. V' produced for Lord Moira, afterwards the Marquess of Hastings, by Sita Ram between 1814-15. Marquess of Hastings, the Governor-General of Bengal and the Commander-in-Chief (r. 1813-23), was accompanied by artist Sita Ram (flourished c.1810-22) to illustrate his journey from Calcutta to Delhi between 1814-15.

Haridwar, located on the right bank of the Ganges river in Uttar Pradesh, is known for the bathing ghat called Harikacharan, or Vishnu's Footprint, at the Gangadwara temple. Idealised view of a bathing ghat and temple in Haridwar. Inscribed below: 'Bathing place at Hurdwar.'
